subject: environmental-science

moments.title: Eunice Foote measures CO₂ heating
moments.body: Foote's experiments, presented at the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 1856 (read by a man because women could not present), show that CO₂ absorbs more solar heat than common air. She speculates that varying atmospheric CO₂ would change Earth's temperature.
moments.takeaway: The greenhouse effect was experimentally demonstrated by a woman three years before Tyndall — and was forgotten.

moments.title: Tyndall measures infrared absorption
moments.body: Tyndall demonstrates that water vapour and CO₂ absorb infrared radiation, identifying the greenhouse mechanism. His more thorough quantitative work establishes the field; Foote's work is rediscovered only in 2010.
moments.takeaway: Two independent demonstrations of the greenhouse effect within three years; the better-funded man's career and credit endured.

moments.title: Arrhenius's CO₂-doubling calculation
moments.body: Arrhenius calculates that doubling atmospheric CO₂ would warm the Earth by ~5-6 °C (modern climate sensitivity: ~3 °C). He spends most of the next year doing the calculations by hand, motivated partly by the cold of a Stockholm winter and recent divorce. He considers the warming a positive future development.
moments.takeaway: The basic mathematics of CO₂-driven climate change was done by 1896. The atmosphere has continued to behave roughly as Arrhenius predicted.

now.title: Climate science today
now.body: Atmospheric CO₂ has risen from ~280 ppm (pre-industrial) to 422 ppm (2024). Global mean temperature is ~1.2 °C above pre-industrial. The mechanism Tyndall and Arrhenius identified has not changed; the magnitude is now well-measured. Climate sensitivity estimates have narrowed to ~2.5-4 °C (IPCC AR6).
now.open_questions: Where exactly does climate sensitivity sit within the range? Cloud feedbacks remain the biggest uncertainty.

reflection: Eunice Foote's 1856 paper was found in a digitised AAAS Proceedings in 2010. The history of science is not fixed; it is constantly rewritten by archive work.
